newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Feb 28.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Feb 28.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH

The Inland Revenue has announced that shares from converging insurers are to be treated in the same way as those from converting building societies. This means that three million Norwich Union members will be able to put the bonus shares they receive from the insurer's four billion stg floatation into personal equity plans without affecting their annual Pep allowances. The Inland Revenue regards shares granted on conversions as being free for Pep purposes because they are not paid for by their recipients.
-- BRITISH LAND IN VENTURE TO BUY GUS PORTFOLIO

British Land property company has formed a 50-50 joint venture to buy 960 million stg of buildings owned by mail order and retailing group Great Universal Stores. More than 90 per cent of the portfolio are high street shops or shopping centres. The property company intends to manage the portfolio actively, selling some units or enhancing their value by buying freeholds or seeking deals with occupying tenants.
-- LASMO PREDICTS MORE TAKEOVER BIDS IN SECTOR

One of the two leading independent oil and gas explorers, Lasmo, expects more bid activity in the sector after Gulf Canada's successful bid for Clyde Petroleum. Chief executive, Joe Darby, has reflected other oil executives' surprise about the premium Gulf offered to win Clyde. Analysts believe other North American predators are continuing to assess the UK sector but are uncertain about the next target.
THE TIMES
-- MARKS AND SPENCER LAYS OUT PLANS FOR 400 MILLION STG OVERSEAS SHOPS SPREE

Marks and Spencer is set to open its largest franchise store within the next month and is planning a 400 million stg programme of store openings around the world over the next three years. Deputy chairman, Keith Oates, said the company had "pressed the accelerator" on overseas expansion. Openings and store expansion is also set to continue in the UK and, because it prefers to own the freehold on its UK stores, spending on expansion is to remain higher in the UK than abroad.
-- ABBEY NATIONAL TO TAKE FORMAL BID FOR SCOTAM

Retail high street bank, Abbey National, has reported a 20 per cent rise in annual pre-tax profits to 1.3 billion stg and will formally bid for mutual insurer Scottish Amicable. Chairman Lord Tugendhat declined to say how much his bid was worth but it is believed that it has been raised from its initial value of 1.4 billion stg to near the rival offer from Prudential of 1.9 billion stg. NatWest have announced it has withdrawn from bidding because the price was too high.
-- SOCIETIES BILL SET TO BE LAW BEFORE ELECTION

The Building Societies Bill is to be laid before Parliament and is expected to become law before the general election. The Bill will give building societies more freedom to expand into new areas such as general insurance and is expected to pass through the Commons unopposed after Shadow Economic Secretary Mike O'Brian gave his backing. However, the Labour Party is to put forward an amendment to have a clause inserted on a two-year rule to discourage so-called "carpetbaggers" from making a quick profit should a society shed its mutual status and become a bank.
THE GUARDIAN
-- WHITBREAD SLIPS LEASH OFF BRANDS

Brewing and leisure giant, Whitbread, has unveiled a shake-up of its restaurant, hotel and leisure operations. The reorganisation follows the news that head of Whitbread's restaurants and leisure division, David Thomas, will replace Peter Jarvis as chief executive. Whitbread is set to create five business groups in the restaurant, hotel and leisure area, which previously operated as a single division. The move is Thomas's attempt to stamp his own identity on the way the company is managed.
-- IMRO SEES WATCHDOG WOES IF LABOUR WINS

Philip Thorpe, chief executive of Imro claims that City watchdogs are experiencing problems recruiting and retaining staff because of uncertainties created by Labour Party plans for change in the governance of the Square Mile. He said there was a danger that a change could create "planning blight" in the Square Mile and he urged future Labour administration to implement any change to City regulation as quickly as possible to limit any damage during a transitional period.
-- BANKER GIVES SINGLE CURRENCY WARNING

Michel Francois-Poncet, chairman of the supervisory board of Groupe Paribas, has warned that companies in Britain, Italy and Spain may be under-estimating the impact of the introduction of the single European currency on their banks. Paribas has plans to be one of the leaders in Euro-denominated products and has set aside 32 million stg against the information technology costs of the arrival of the single currency.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- CENTRICA WANTS SELECTIVE PRICE CUTS TO BEAT OFF RIVALS

Former British Gas supply business, Centrica, is in talks with Clare Spottiswoode, industry regulator, in its drive to gain approval to make the first selective price cuts to customers for decades. Chief executive, Roy Gardner, has submitted a detailed package of discounts to the regulator affecting some of the 500,000 homes taking part in the first trail of domestic competition in the South-west of England.
-- BRITISH SHARE OF NEW INVESTMENT IN EU 'DECLINING'

Figures from the UN's Conference on Trade and Development (Unctad) shows that the British share of new overseas investment in the EU is in decline. This adds weight to business leaders' fears that the tide of anti-European feeling in the Conservative Party will harm inward investment prospects. A speech by Adair Turner, director general of the CBI, is to put forward the argument that even if the UK does not join the single currency, it is essential for the sake of business for the Government to strike a positive tone.
-- NEW DELAYS HIT CABLE AND WIRELESS'S OFFSPRING

Cable and Wireless is faced with delays in recruiting senior executives to join the board of the five billion stg company it is forming through its merger of its Mercury Communications subsidiary with three cable operators. Sources say that headhunters bought in by C&W have yet to finalise shortlists of applicants for some of the top posts. The news will add speculation that the task of creating C&W Communications is slipping behind schedule.
